assessment.nobel_worthiness: Introduced heterogeneous firms, selective exporting and the reallocation channel into trade theory. This changed how gains from trade are modelled, measured and taken to firm-level data. It is a clear conceptual advance beyond the new trade theory already recognised in 2008, with large empirical and policy reach.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the core model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple link it to exporting versus FDI, and Helpman's wider work on firms and trade adds depth. Redding's contributions are better described as quantitative and spatial extensions than as the central discovery, so I limit the proposal to two.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation in firm-level data across many countries, and the framework is standard in graduate teaching and policy modelling. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to pair Helpman with the growth and politics work in B047 instead.
Whether Redding or other contributors such as Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum should be treated as co-originators.
My view of the relative weight of the extensive-margin results versus the quantitative-trade literature is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reshaped understanding of how technology, tasks and import competition change labour demand, polarisation and local labour markets. It combines a conceptual framework (skills and tasks) with credible quasi-experimental evidence (China shock) on big societal questions.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz are central to skill-biased and task-based change and to the education–technology race. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are central to the trade-shock evidence. Hanson and Katz round out the two strands. Dorn is a key coauthor on the trade shock, and the task framework's other originators are not on the list, so attribution is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of replication, extension and debate, including refinements to the China-shock estimates. Mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: Task-framework originators outside the credited names complicate the attribution.
Overlap with recent prizes on labour and economic history (2023) and on technology and institutions (2024).
Debate over the persistence of trade-shock effects and over measurement choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Made estimation of demand and supply in differentiated-product markets practical (BLP), and developed dynamic oligopoly models and estimation. These methods are used daily in merger review, antitrust and empirical industrial organisation, and extend across fields.
assessment.attribution: The BLP contribution is clearly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, with Pakes also leading the dynamic-games work (Ericson–Pakes, Olley–Pakes). Bresnahan's contributions to empirical IO and Reiss's contributions are important but distinct strands. A three-person limit forces exclusions.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and is thoroughly confirmed, with decades of use and methodological refinement. Timing is very mature.
uncertainties: Bundling heterogeneous strands (demand estimation, production-function estimation, dynamics) makes the discovery boundary fuzzy.
Choosing among Bresnahan, Levinsohn and Berry is arguable.
Methodological prizes may be weighed against substantive findings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built the modern framework for analysing monetary policy: nominal rigidities, the New Keynesian Phillips curve, rules-based policy and the welfare-based approach to central banking. Its practical impact on central-bank practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: Woodford and Gali supply the canonical theoretical synthesis. Taylor supplies the policy rule and staggered-contract work. Calvo, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, and Smets are also strongly arguable, and many co-creators exceed three seats, so credit allocation is the weak point.
assessment.maturity: Developed from the 1980s to the 2000s and tested through several policy regimes, including the post-2008 and post-2021 episodes, which raise questions about the framework's limits.
uncertainties: Large number of plausible contributors and a strong chance that the trio is wrong.
Post-pandemic inflation exposed limits of the framework, though the core contribution remains.
Overlap with prior macro prizes (Lucas, Prescott, Sargent, Bernanke).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reframed inference around what data can reveal under credible, weak assumptions. Partial identification and bounds inform treatment-effect and policy analysis, and moment-inequality methods are used in structural work. It is a deep conceptual contribution to empirical science.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator (bounds, the identification problem). Tamer led the move to set identification and moment inequalities in econometric models. Molinari is a major contemporary contributor but later in the line.
assessment.maturity: Manski's work goes back to the late 1980s with growing adoption. Applied uptake is mixed relative to the theoretical influence.
uncertainties: Applied influence is narrower than that of the causal-inference prize in 2021.
Selecting Tamer versus Molinari is a judgment call.
Recent econometrics prizes may reduce appetite for another methods award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Provided micro-data evidence that household leverage and credit supply drive housing booms, consumption collapses and recessions. It transformed understanding of the financial crisis and household balance-sheet channels, and has major policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the core, consistent coauthors with clear joint credit. Campbell's household-finance work is related but a distinct contribution, so I leave him out.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of work and replication, with some debate over identification and credit-supply measures. Reasonably mature but newer than other candidates.
uncertainties: Some findings, such as the role of credit supply versus expectations, remain contested.
The 2022 prize recognised banking and financial crises, creating thematic overlap.
May be judged slightly early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Brought rigorous empirical and sufficient-statistics methods to optimal taxation and public policy, connecting behavioural elasticities to welfare. Strong policy influence and a data-driven approach across big questions.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the central figure on taxable income, optimal-tax theory and top-incomes evidence. Chetty's sufficient-statistics approach is distinct and also credited elsewhere. Feldstein, who originated the elasticity-of-taxable-income approach, is deceased and not eligible, and Slemrod and Stantcheva are real contributors, so attribution is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Substantial but partly recent. The sufficient-statistics programme and some empirical results are still under evaluation.
uncertainties: Overlap with B039 and B044, with Saez and Chetty appearing in several candidates.
Chetty's career stage may argue for waiting.
Disagreement about the robustness of elasticity estimates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion defined information design: how a sender can optimally shape signals. It unified a range of communication and mechanism problems, with applications in law, platforms, regulation and political economy.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow created the baseline model. Morris, with Bergemann, developed the robust information-design approach and brought earlier foundational work on higher-order beliefs. Bergemann is arguably as strong as Gentzkow for the extended literature, so the choice is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen years since the 2011 paper, with rapid growth, but the empirical validation and field impact are less established than for older candidates.
uncertainties: Theoretical influence is large but real-world application is still developing.
Overlap with the 2020 auction-theory and 2007 mechanism-design prizes.
Gentzkow versus Bergemann is a difficult attribution call.
